around.headline: Man loses ₹67,000 after sharing bank details with the thief who stole his mother's phone on a train
around.summary: A Bengaluru man's family lost ₹67,000 after he shared bank account details connected to a phone stolen from his mother on a train. Whoever contacts you about a stolen phone — even claiming to be your bank or the police — never share account numbers, card details, or OTPs over a call or message; verify independently by calling your bank's official number yourself.

around.headline: Metro death revives calls for platform safety doors as Namma Metro logs 59 track incidents since 2012
around.summary: A man died after going onto the tracks at a Bengaluru metro station, reviving demands for platform screen doors; officials note Namma Metro has recorded 59 track-related incidents since 2012. Stand well back from the yellow line while waiting, especially on crowded platforms.
around.source: The Times of India, The Hindu

around.headline: 100+ localities face 15-hour Cauvery water supply disruption on July 31
around.summary: More than 100 Bengaluru localities will have no Cauvery water supply for 15 hours on July 31 for maintenance work. Store water in advance if your area is affected — check with your local BWSSB office or ward for the exact list.

around.headline: ₹450-crore Outer Ring Road revamp to add dedicated bus and cycle lanes, gig-worker hubs
around.summary: The ORR makeover will include dedicated bus and cycle lanes, smart bus stops, and gig-worker hubs with charging points and Wi-Fi under flyovers. Expect construction disruption along the corridor as work rolls out.

around.headline: CCTV and police verification made mandatory for homestays under revamped Karnataka rules
around.summary: Karnataka has revamped homestay regulations to require CCTV coverage and police checks on operators. If you're booking a homestay, this is now a baseline safety standard you can reasonably expect and ask about.

around.headline: Oil prices ease, but Strait of Hormuz tensions remain the wildcard
around.summary: Crude prices have retreated for now even as US-Saudi strikes on Iran-aligned targets in Iraq and missile interceptions keep Gulf tensions high, with the Strait of Hormuz still a risk to watch. A flare-up there could push petrol and diesel prices back up quickly, so it's worth timing big fuel-ups if you're due for one.

street_smart.title: Your family member's phone gets stolen on a train. Minutes later, a call comes in about the linked bank account — saying it needs to be 'verified' or 'secured' right away. What do you do?
street_smart.based_on: Real case reported today: a Bengaluru man's family lost ₹67,000 after sharing bank details connected to a phone stolen from his mother on a train. The source doesn't detail exactly how the request for details reached him, so this scenario is built around the standard, well-documented playbook for this kind of follow-up fraud, not a guess at the specific call script used (The Times of India).
street_smart.situation: The phone is gone, you're rattled, and someone on the line sounds urgent and official about protecting the account tied to it.

choices.text: Hang up, and independently call your bank using the number printed on your card or their official website/app — not any number the caller gives you — to freeze the card and account yourself.
choices.feedback: Correct. Banks never call asking you to read out OTPs, full card numbers, or CVVs. Freezing the account yourself through a number you looked up independently closes the loop the thief is trying to open, and it's the fastest real way to stop money moving.

choices.text: Share the account number and OTP since the caller already seems to know the phone was stolen, so it feels like they must be genuine.
choices.feedback: This is the trap. Knowing a phone was just stolen is easy for a thief to fake urgency with — it's not proof they're your bank. An OTP is the one thing that actually authorises a transaction; sharing it is what turns a stolen phone into a drained account.

choices.text: Ignore the call completely and deal with it later once you've calmed down.
choices.feedback: Better than sharing details, but every minute you wait gives more time for the thief to act. Blocking the SIM and freezing the account should happen immediately, not 'later.'

choices.text: Ask the caller to prove who they are by texting you an ID number, then proceed based on that.
choices.feedback: A caller can text you anything that looks official — a fabricated employee ID proves nothing. The only reliable verification is you initiating contact through a number you found independently, not trusting anything the caller provides.

takeaways: If a phone is stolen, immediately block its SIM (via your telecom's app/helpline) and freeze linked bank accounts and UPI using your bank's app or a number you look up yourself — never one given by a caller.
No bank, telecom company, or police officer will ever ask you to read out an OTP, CVV, or full card number over a call or message — that request alone means it's a scam.
Report the theft and any fraud at cybercrime.gov.in or by calling 1930, and use ceir.gov.in to blacklist the stolen phone's IMEI so it can't be reused.

quiz.why: The Lok Sabha is currently debating a new anti-paper-leak law, following youth protests over exam paper leaks this year.

quiz.q: If your phone is stolen, which government portal lets you block it nationwide using its IMEI number?
quiz.why: CEIR (ceir.gov.in) lets you blacklist a stolen phone's IMEI so it can't be reused on any network, even with a new SIM.
